question: Which common, lightweight device uses two small prongs to deliver low-flow oxygen right into a patient's nostrils?
explanation: You'll see nasal cannulas everywhere in the ward! They're the standard, comfortable choice for giving patients a little extra oxygen through their nose. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h1)

question: As a nurse, why would you start a patient on nasal oxygen therapy?

options.A: To treat tissue hypoxia and raise low blood oxygen levels
options.B: To deliver high-pressure aerosolized medications to the lungs
options.C: To completely replace normal breathing mechanics during sleep
options.D: To prevent the patient from experiencing dry mouth overnight

explanation: Spot on! We give oxygen when the body's tissues aren't getting enough of it (hypoxia), helping to bring those blood oxygen levels back up to a safe place. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h1)

question: What equipment do you attach directly to an oxygen source to control how fast the gas flows?
explanation: The flow meter is your best friend for control—it lets you accurately dial in the exact liters per minute prescribed for your patient. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h2)

question: When do you typically hook up a humidification bottle filled with sterile water to an oxygen setup?

options.A: Only when the patient is diagnosed with an active lung infection
options.B: Whenever oxygen is delivered at any flow rate below one liter
options.C: When delivering higher flow rates that can dry the nasal passages
options.D: To cool the temperature of the gas before it enters the nose

explanation: Medical oxygen is very dry and can irritate the nose at higher flows. Adding sterile water for humidification keeps your patient nice and comfortable! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h2)

question: What is the best bed position for a patient struggling to breathe who needs supplemental oxygen?

options.A: Prone position facing down on the bed
options.C: Flat on the back with legs slightly raised

explanation: Sitting upright in Semi- or High-Fowler's position lets gravity help expand the lungs fully, making every breath much easier for your patient. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h3)

question: You notice raw, red skin inside a patient's nostrils while getting ready to put on a nasal cannula. What should you do first?

options.A: Scrub the irritated skin vigorously with an antiseptic alcohol wipe
options.B: Switch the patient immediately to an invasive mechanical ventilator
options.C: Refuse to start the oxygen therapy until the skin is completely healed
options.D: Document the finding, apply a water-based lubricant if ordered, and monitor the area closely

explanation: Always check and document skin status! Protecting sore areas with safe, water-based lubricants helps prevent further friction without stopping vital oxygen. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h3)

question: How should the little prongs of a nasal cannula face when you put them into a patient's nose?
explanation: They are shaped to match human anatomy! Pointing them downward ensures they slide comfortably along the natural curve of the nasal passages. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h4)

question: Why is it smart to check that gas is actually flowing out of the cannula prongs before placing them on the patient?

options.A: To measure the exact oxygen percentage in the room air
options.B: To confirm the equipment works and gas is actively delivering
options.C: To clear out any trapped dust from the manufacturing factory
options.D: To warm up the cold gas before it touches the sensitive nasal lining

explanation: A quick check saves a lot of trouble—you want to make sure there isn't a kinked tube or a closed valve blocking air before it reaches your patient. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h4)

question: What is the usual maximum flow rate recommended for a standard nasal cannula?
explanation: We usually stick to 1 to 6 Liters per minute for standard cannulas. Going higher mostly just dries out the nose without giving extra benefits. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h5)

question: Why does the actual amount of oxygen (FiO2) a patient receives from a nasal cannula vary from person to person?

options.A: Different hospitals calibrate their wall oxygen outlets to different pressures
options.B: It depends on the patient's breathing rate and depth, which mixes room air with the oxygen
options.C: Patients absorb oxygen at different speeds through their skin
options.D: The plastic tubing stretches or shrinks based on the room temperature

explanation: Because a nasal cannula is an open system, patients breathe in regular room air right along with the oxygen. How fast or deep they breathe changes the exact mix! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h5)

question: What is an important daily nursing task for a patient on continuous nasal cannula oxygen?

options.A: Inspecting skin behind the ears and providing nasal hygiene
options.B: Keeping the patient strictly confined to bedrest
options.C: Changing the wall flow meter every four hours
options.D: Washing the entire length of the plastic tubing with soap

explanation: Plastic tubing can rub against delicate skin behind the ears and in the nose. Regular checks and basic hygiene keep your patient safe and comfortable. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h6)

question: Your patient on a nasal cannula complains of a dry, sore throat and a mild nosebleed. What is your best nursing action?

options.A: Increase the oxygen flow rate to flush the nasal passages
options.B: Recommend adding humidification to the oxygen setup as prescribed
options.C: Remove the oxygen permanently and document refusal of care
options.D: Switch the patient to a tight-fitting non-rebreather mask

explanation: Dry medical gas can be tough on delicate mucous membranes. Adding moisture (humidification) is the perfect fix to soothe that dryness and irritation. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h6)

question: Which of these substances should you NEVER use to soothe dry nostrils during oxygen therapy because of fire risks?
explanation: Never use petroleum-based products around oxygen! They are flammable and can easily catch fire in an oxygen-rich environment—always stick to water-based options. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h7)

question: Why do oxygen cylinders and wall outlets always need strict 'No Smoking' safety signs nearby?

options.A: Oxygen strongly supports combustion and makes fires spread rapidly
options.B: Tobacco smoke clogs the small holes in the nasal cannula prongs
options.C: Smoking interferes with the machine's internal electrical circuits
options.D: The smell of smoke ruins the purity of the medical gas supply

explanation: Oxygen itself doesn't burn, but it feeds fires aggressively. Even a tiny spark can turn into a massive flame in seconds around supplemental oxygen! [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h7)
